building.local_amendments_note: State law bars a municipality from requiring building code provisions that differ from the State Building Code (Minn. Stat. 326B.121, quoted in the state pack). The city's plan review page lists the 2020 Minnesota State Building Code first under 'Codes and ordinances', with Title 5 (Building Code) and Title 20 (Zoning) of the Minneapolis Code of Ordinances. Title 5 itself sits on Municode, which refuses automated access (HTTP 403), so the adopting section was not read.

[...] Codes and ordinances: 2020 Minnesota State Building Code; Guide to the Minnesota State Building Code; Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Title 5; Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Title 20
building.edition_quote: The 2020 Minnesota State Building Code is effective March 31, 2020, except for the Minnesota Mechanical Fuel Gas Code, which is effective April 6, 2020. It is the minimum construction standard throughout all of Minnesota. Although it is not enforceable by municipalities unless it is adopted by local ordinance, it creates a level playing field for the construction industry by establishing the Minnesota State Building Code as the standard for the construction of all buildings in the state. [...] The 2020 Minnesota Building Code remains in effect with no other charges [sic].

The Department of Labor and Industry's docket for chapter 1305 (a code based on the 2024 International Building Code) shows a Request for Comments published January 21, 2025 and every later step, including the effective date, 'To be determined' (re-read 2026-11-24). The Plumbing Board's page says 'There is currently no active rulemaking', and lists a 2024 UPC ad hoc rulemaking committee.

fixtures.basis: Minneapolis cannot amend the counts: the State Building Code supersedes any municipal building code and a municipality must not require provisions that differ from it (Minn. Stat. 326B.121, state pack). The city's plan review page names the 2020 Minnesota State Building Code as the code it reviews plans against, and no city page read mentions a local toilet-count rule. Minneapolis Code Title 5 was not read (Municode blocks automated access), so 'no city amendment' rests on the statute and the city's pages, not on the ordinance text. The state pack's worked examples stand.
fixtures.quote: (b) The State Building Code supersedes the building code of any municipality. [...] (c) A municipality must not by ordinance, or through development agreement, require building code provisions regulating components or systems of any structure that are different from any provision of the State Building Code. [quoted from the state pack, read 2026-11-24]

permit.exempt_list_quote: Subp. 4. Work exempt from permit. Exemptions from permit requirements of the code do not authorize work to be done in any manner in violation of the code or any other laws or ordinances of this jurisdiction. Permits shall not be required for the following: A. Building: (1) one-story detached accessory structures, used as tool and storage sheds, playhouses, and similar uses, provided the floor area does not exceed 200 square feet (18.58 m2); (2) fences not over seven feet (2,134 mm) high; (3) oil derricks; (4) retaining walls that are not over four feet (1,219 mm) in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, unless supporting a surcharge or impounding Class I, II, or III-A liquids; (5) water tanks supported directly upon grade if the capacity does not exceed 5,000 gallons (18,927 L) and the ratio of height to diameter or width does not exceed 2 to 1; (6) sidewalks and driveways that are not part of an accessible route; (7) decks and platforms not more than 30 inches (762 mm) above adjacent grade and not attached to a structure with frost footings and which is not part of an accessible route; (8) painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, countertops, and similar finish work; (9) temporary motion picture, television, and theater stage sets and scenery; (10) prefabricated swimming pools [...]; (11) window awnings [...]; (12) movable cases, counters, and partitions not over five feet, nine inches (1,753 mm) in height; (13) swings and other playground equipment; and (14) electric substation facilities [...]. Unless otherwise exempted, plumbing, electrical, and mechanical permits are required for subitems (1) to (14).

[...] Whereas, the City of Minneapolis has amended City code on this day to eliminate all requirements to provide gender-specific single-user restrooms; [...] Now, Therefore, Be It Resolved by The City Council of The City of Minneapolis: That the City of Minneapolis strongly encourages businesses, educational facilities, and buildings of every description within Minneapolis who offer single-user restrooms for use by employees and/or the public to provide such facilities in a gender-neutral manner wherever possible. restrooms_city.note: No city rule that adds to the state rule was found (one web search). What was found is a City Council resolution of September 19, 2014 that encourages, and does not require, gender-neutral single-user restrooms, and says the city amended its code the same day to remove its own requirements for gender-specific single-user restrooms. It was read on a copy of the council proceedings page hosted by OutFront Minnesota, not on a city site. The amended ordinance was not read (Municode blocks automated access). Since then the state code itself requires single-user rooms to be identified for use by either sex (state pack). This is 'none found', not 'none exists'.

public_wage.city_rule: Minneapolis has its own prevailing wage ordinance (Code of Ordinances, Title 2, Chapter 24). It applies to City construction projects of $50,000 or more where the City contracts directly with a general contractor for public improvements; it may not cover development projects under a development agreement. Bids and contracts incorporate federal labor standards and prevailing wage provisions. Enforced by the Contract Compliance Division of the Civil Rights department, 612-673-3012.
public_wage.city_rule_quote: You must pay the prevailing wage if you want to get a City construction contract for more than $50,000. [...] The City's prevailing wage ordinance applies to City construction projects: That are greater than or equal to $50,000, and Where the City has a direct contract with a general contractor for public improvements. It may not cover development projects where the City enters into a development agreement. | Fact sheet: All applicable invitations (bids, RFPs, or best value solicitations) and contracts will incorporate federal labor standards and prevailing wage provisions and all contractors and subcontractors must comply with these. [...] Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Title 2, Chapter 24.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Minneapolis job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Minnesota rules Minneapolis enforces.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Minneapolis office towers, university buildings, hospitals and restaurants, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Minnesota's building rules set the number of toilets by how many people use the building. Minneapolis enforces them as the state writes them, because cities may not change the state building rules. The table below shows what that means.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Minneapolis says almost all projects need a building permit before work starts. The work that needs none is listed in the state building rules, which the city points to. That list includes "painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, countertops, and similar finish work" and "movable cases, counters, and partitions not over five feet, nine inches" in height. It doesn't name toilet partitions, and neither do the city's own examples of exempt interior work. Ask Minneapolis Construction Code Services (612-673-3000) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** a one-person restroom must be marked for use by either sex. Minnesota's building rules call for separate men's and women's rooms once a space holds more than 25 people, and they don't yet set out how a shared all-gender room with stalls can take their place, so ask Minneapolis Construction Code Services before planning one. No Minnesota law limits who may use which restroom.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, the building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20. Your architect or Minneapolis Construction Code Services sets the final number.
page.install_rule: Building permits in Minneapolis come from the city's Construction Code Services. Building work in Minneapolis needs the applicable state and city contractor licenses, so ask the city whether partition installation falls under one of its license classes. Minnesota has no skills license for this work, but a contractor doing commercial construction who doesn't hold a residential contractor license registers with the state Department of Labor and Industry. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor doing commercial work in Minnesota registers with the state Department of Labor and Industry.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on projects paid for in whole or in part with state money, including state buildings, colleges and schools, Minnesota law requires at least the wage the state certifies for each trade in each county, once the job costs $2,500 with one trade or $25,000 with several. For a carpenter on commercial building work in Hennepin County that is $51.56 an hour plus $29.84 in benefits. Minneapolis has its own rule too: contractors on city construction contracts of $50,000 or more must pay the prevailing wage.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 9.025% in Minneapolis: 6.875% state, 0.5% city, 0.15% Hennepin County, 0.5% county transit and 1% in two metro area taxes (0.75% for transportation and 0.25% for housing).
page.buyers_extra: - **Downtown office towers and skyway-level tenants:** one material and finish repeated floor after floor, with ceiling-hung or overhead braced stalls for restrooms that see heavy weekday traffic.

Checked 2026-11-24.

- Sales tax in Minneapolis: Minnesota Department of Revenue, [Local Sales and Use Tax Rate Guide, effective October 1 to December 31, 2026](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2026-08/local-sales-and-use-tax-rate-guide-2026-q4.pdf) (Minneapolis 9.025%), [Sales Tax Fact Sheet 164M, Minneapolis Special Local Taxes](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2025-02/fs164m.pdf) (the parts by name) and [Local Sales Tax Notices](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/local-sales-tax-notices) (metro area taxes from October 1, 2023; Hennepin County transit tax from October 1, 2017). Checked 2026-11-24.

- Minneapolis wage rule on city contracts: City of Minneapolis Contract Compliance Division, [Prevailing wage](https://www.minneapolismn.gov/business-services/doing-business-with-the-city/contract-compliance/prevailing-wage/) and the [City Prevailing Wage Fact Sheet](https://www.minneapolismn.gov/media/-www-content-assets/documents/City-Prevailing-Wage-Fact-Sheet.pdf) (Minneapolis Code of Ordinances, Title 2, Chapter 24). page.official_names: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design; 2020 Minnesota Accessibility Code (Minnesota Rules chapter 1341: 2018 IBC Chapter 11 and ICC/ANSI A117.1-2009 with Minnesota amendments); 2020 Minnesota Building Code (Minnesota Rules chapter 1305: 2018 International Building Code with Minnesota amendments, in force since March 31, 2020); 2020 Minnesota Plumbing Code (Minnesota Rules chapter 4714: 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code with Minnesota amendments, in force since December 17, 2021); Minnesota Rules chapter 1300 (Minnesota Building Code Administration) for permits; all enforced in Minneapolis by Construction Code Services without local amendments; NFPA 286 for HDPE.
notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether replacing or adding anchored toilet partitions in an existing commercial restroom needs a Minneapolis building permit, or falls under 'similar finish work' or 'movable ... partitions not over five feet, nine inches' in Minnesota Rules 1300.0120 (Construction Code Services, 612-673-3000).

Minneapolis Code of Ordinances (Title 5 building code, Title 2 Chapter 24 prevailing wage, contractor licence chapters) sits on Municode, which refuses automated access: the adopting section, the wage ordinance and the licence classes were not read. Browser check.
The permit bullet quotes two items of the state's exempt-work list word for word; the height in the second is five feet, nine inches.

City wage rule: the city's pages give the $50,000 threshold but don't name the rate schedule for city-funded jobs; they link to federal wage determinations. The federal Hennepin County building rate for carpenters (MN20260053, modification 2) equals the state rate, $51.56 plus $29.84. Confirm with the Contract Compliance Division, 612-673-3012.

The carpenter rate has dated steps: $48.56 from December 22, 2025 and $51.56 from May 4, 2026. The current certification is dated December 22, 2025 (revised February 9, 2026); recheck when the next one is published.

Not in page text: a City Council resolution of September 19, 2014 (2014R-394) encourages gender-neutral single-user restrooms and says the city removed its own requirements for gender-specific single-user rooms that day. It was read on a copy hosted by OutFront Minnesota, not a city site, and it sets no requirement.
Sales tax: no change for Minneapolis is announced on the Department of Revenue's notices page; the first-quarter 2027 rate guide wasn't posted yet. Recheck in December.
No code change has a date: the state's move to a code based on the 2024 International Building Code is still in rulemaking, and the Plumbing Board lists no active rulemaking.
The buyers bullet on downtown towers and the four building types in the lead are editorial, not sourced.
The restroom bullet is the state pack's, with 'your local building official' replaced by Minneapolis Construction Code Services; the city adds no rule.
